lessons.title: Create a character
lessons.tip: A fiction character feels real when we know what they want, what stops them, and one small detail only they have. Give them a want (to win a race), a flaw (too proud to ask for help) and a habit or an object (always twists a ring). Then show them making a choice.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Setting and mood
lessons.tip: Setting is where and when a scene happens. It also sets the mood: a quiet lake feels calm, a crowded station feels tense. Choose two or three details that create the feeling you want, instead of describing everything.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)

lessons.title: Use the five senses
lessons.tip: Good description uses all five senses, not only sight: what we see, hear, smell, taste and touch. One precise detail can make a scene alive. “The bread smelled of warm butter” tells more than “The bread was nice.”
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Show, don’t tell
lessons.tip: Telling states a feeling: “He was nervous.” Showing lets the reader see it: “His hands shook as he checked the clock again.” Show the important moments through actions, words and the body. Use telling for small, quick facts.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Write dialogue
lessons.tip: Dialogue should sound like real people: short lines, interruptions, and a different voice for each speaker. Use “said” for most lines, and start a new paragraph for each new speaker. Good dialogue also shows what people want or hide.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Point of view
lessons.tip: Point of view (POV) is who tells the story. First person uses “I”: we know only what the narrator knows. Third person limited uses “he” or “she” but stays close to one character’s thoughts. Omniscient sees into everyone’s mind. Pick one and stay with it in a scene.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Plot shape
lessons.tip: A simple plot has a beginning (meet the character and the problem), a rising middle (things get harder), a climax (the biggest moment) and an ending (what changes). Each step should follow from the one before: because of this, then that.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Beginnings and endings
lessons.tip: Begin as close to the action as you can: a moment, a question, a problem. Skip long background. End with a change, not a summary: show what is different for the character now. A good ending feels both surprising and right.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Find a voice
lessons.tip: Voice is the way a story sounds: the choice of words, the length of sentences and the attitude behind them. A cheerful narrator and a tired narrator describe the same street differently. Choose a voice that fits the story and keep it steady. Read your pages aloud: if a sentence sounds like someone else, rewrite it in the voice you chose.
sources: Public-domain essays and handbooks on style and fiction craft (concepts only; no text copied)
Common creative-writing workshop practice: concrete detail, subtext, scene and summary, revision (original wording)

lessons.title: Specific, surprising details
lessons.tip: A detail is specific when only this person or place could have it. “A car” is general; “a green car with one brown door” is specific. Choose details that tell the reader something about character or feeling, not just appearance. One surprising detail can do more than five ordinary ones. Ask of every detail: What does this show?
sources: Public-domain essays and handbooks on style and fiction craft (concepts only; no text copied)
Common creative-writing workshop practice: concrete detail, subtext, scene and summary, revision (original wording)

lessons.title: Simile, metaphor, and when to stop
lessons.tip: A simile compares with “like” or “as”: “Her laugh was like a door slamming.” A metaphor says one thing is another: “The city was a machine.” Fresh comparisons help readers see. Avoid clichés such as “cold as ice.” Use one strong image rather than three weak ones, and make sure the comparison fits the mood of the scene.

lessons.title: Conflict and stakes
lessons.tip: A story moves when someone wants something and something stands in the way. That is conflict. The obstacle can be a person, a rule, a place or a fear inside the character. Stakes are what the character could lose or win. Raise the stakes slowly: let the reader see why it matters. If nothing could be lost, there is little to read for.

lessons.title: Say it without saying it
lessons.tip: In real life people often do not say what they mean. Subtext is the meaning under the words. In dialogue, let characters talk about one thing while feeling another. Use actions and objects to carry the feeling. In the kitchen scene, Jun puts the bag where he can reach it quickly: the words are polite, but the action says he may leave. Do not explain the subtext; trust the reader.

lessons.title: Control the pace
lessons.tip: Pace is how fast the story moves. Summary covers time quickly: “For three weeks she wrote every night.” A scene slows down and shows moment by moment, with dialogue and detail. Use summary for the in-between and scenes for what matters most. Short sentences speed up the action; longer ones slow the mood. If the story drags, cut or summarize; if it rushes, expand the key moment into a scene.

lessons.title: Revise: cut, move, sharpen
lessons.tip: Writing becomes good in revision. First read the whole draft for shape: does it have a clear want, an obstacle and a change? Then cut what repeats or does not matter. Move parts to a better place. Last, sharpen sentences: replace weak words such as “really” and “very,” and choose stronger verbs. Revise in rounds, one job at a time, and put the draft away for a day between rounds.

lessons.title: Share your work and receive feedback
lessons.tip: Feedback helps you see what you cannot see. Tell readers what kind of help you want: “Is the ending clear?” Listen without defending. Notice where several readers agree; that is probably a real problem. When you give feedback, begin with what works, name one thing that confused you, and describe your reaction rather than ordering a change: “I got lost in the middle” is more useful than “Rewrite the middle.”

lessons.title: Narrative distance
lessons.tip: Narrative distance is how close the narrator stands to a character’s mind. Close distance uses thoughts and sensations: “I have wasted all of it.” Far distance summarizes from above: “The town learned to live without the mill.” Move between them on purpose. Close distance builds feeling at key moments; far distance covers time and context quickly. A sudden jump you did not intend confuses readers.

lessons.title: Beyond three acts
lessons.tip: Chronological order is only one choice. A frame story wraps a tale inside another situation. A braided structure alternates two timelines. A fragmented structure presents pieces that the reader assembles. Each choice creates questions: what does the reader know first? Choose a structure that serves your theme, and make the connections between parts clear enough that readers feel guided, not lost.

lessons.title: Theme and motif
lessons.tip: Theme is the underlying idea a story explores, such as loyalty or loss. A motif is an image, sound or object that returns and gathers meaning: a broken clock, a door left open. Do not state the theme; let the motif carry it. Introduce the motif early, vary it with each return, and let its final appearance change its meaning. If a motif appears only once, it is a detail, not a motif.

lessons.title: Unreliable narrators and irony
lessons.tip: An unreliable narrator is one whose account the reader cannot fully trust, because of bias, ignorance, self-deception or deliberate lies. The reader senses the gap between what the narrator says and what the facts show. That gap is dramatic irony. To build it, give the narrator a motive for bending the truth and plant small signals: contradictions, defensive overstatements, details the narrator does not understand. Do not announce the lie; let the reader find it.

lessons.title: Sentence rhythm and syntax
lessons.tip: Variety makes prose alive. Short sentences strike; long sentences accumulate, carry feeling or hold a moment open. Use parallel structure to build momentum, and a sudden short sentence to break it. Place the important word at the end, where the stress falls. Read aloud and mark where your breath stops. If every sentence has the same length and shape, rhythm dies; if every sentence is a flourish, nothing stands out.

lessons.title: Research without losing the story
lessons.tip: Good fiction feels true. Research the details your story depends on: a profession, a place, a period. Interview people, read primary sources, visit if you can. But research serves the story. Choose the few telling details, not everything you learned. Check facts that a reader could easily check, and ask someone from the community you write about to read it. If you are not sure you can portray a group fairly, listen first and write with care.

lessons.title: Draft a long project
lessons.tip: A long project needs routines. Set a regular time and a realistic target, such as 300 words a day. Write the first draft without stopping to polish; leave notes for yourself in brackets. Outline loosely: know the next three scenes. Keep a project file with names, timeline and open questions. Finish the draft before you rewrite; the shape appears only when there is something to shape. Reward finished pages, not perfect ones.

lessons.title: The final edit and sharing
lessons.tip: Before you share a finished piece, do three passes. First pass: structure and scenes; cut what does not move the story. Second: sentences; strengthen verbs, remove repetition, vary rhythm. Third: proofreading; check spelling, punctuation and consistency of names and facts. Read the piece aloud and on a different screen or on paper. Then choose where to share it: a trusted reader, a workshop, a contest, a magazine. Read the rules of each place carefully and follow them.
